SECTION: Requirements for Good Formwork (Pages 3-4)

TOPICS: formwork requirements, formwork classification, structural integrity, material properties, economic considerations, formwork systems

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- A good formwork should be strong enough to withstand all types of dead and live loads (Page 3)
- Formwork must be rigidly constructed and efficiently propped and braced both horizontally and vertically (Page 3)
- Joints should be tight against leakage of cement grout (Page 3)
- Construction should permit removal of parts in desired sequences without damaging concrete (Page 3)
- Material should be cheap, easily available, and suitable for reuse (Page 3)
- Formwork should be set accurately to desired lines and levels with a plane surface (Page 3)
- Formwork should be as light as possible (Page 3)
- Material should not warp or distort when exposed to elements (Page 3)
- Formwork should rest on a firm base (Page 3)
- To effect economy, building plans should imply minimum variations in room sizes and floor areas (Page 3)
- Design should use slender sections economically (Page 3)
- Minimum sawing and cutting of wooden pieces should be made to enable reuse (Page 3)
- Conventional formwork is built on-site from timber, plywood, or moisture-resistant particleboard (Page 4)
- Conventional formwork is easy to produce but time-consuming for larger structures and has a short lifespan (Page 4)
- Modern-day formworks are mostly modular, designed for speed, efficiency, increased accuracy, and waste minimization (Page 4)
- The main types of modern-day formwork systems listed are Table form/flying form, System column formwork, Horizontal panel, Slip form, and Tunnel form (Page 4)
- Engineered/Pre-fabricated Formworks are built from prefabricated modules with a metal frame (steel or aluminium) (Page 4)
- The two major advantages of engineered formwork are speed of construction and lower life-cycle costs (Page 4)
- If the covering is made of steel or aluminium, the form can achieve up to two thousand uses depending on care and applications (Page 4)

pages.ocr_text: INTRODUCTION TO FORMWORK What is Formwork? Formwork in construction is the use of support structures and moulds to create structures out of concrete which is poured into the moulds. Formwork can be made using moulds out of steel, wood, aluminium and/or prefabricated forms. Formwork is an ancillary construction, used as a mould for a structure. Into this mould, fresh concrete is placed only to harden subsequently. The construction of formwork takes time and involves expenditure up to 20 to  $25\%$  of the cost of the structure or even more. The operation of removing the formwork is known as stripping. Stripped formwork can be reused. Reusable forms are known as panel forms and non-usable are called stationary forms. Formwork is designed according to The ACI document SP-4.

This page provides an overview of circular and octagonal column formwork, detailing various construction methods including fabricated steel and timber sheathing. It describes two primary types of columns: a vertical steel two-piece form column with bolted joints and a vertical timber sheathing column with wedges. The page includes text outlining the materials and assembly techniques, along with figures showing cross-sectional diagrams and photographs of the actual column forms in use on construction sites.

**Text Evidence:**
- Circular column formwork can be made from fabricated steel (usually two pieces with a hinge), fibre cement pipes, or timber sheathing.
- Fabricated steel columns often have bolted joints and stiffener ribs.
- Timber sheathing columns require corner infill pieces or metal straps to eliminate the need for infills.
- Fibre cement pipes are left in place as permanent formwork.

**Text Evidence:**

- Forces may be wind or impact, occurring from collisions with concrete buckets or cranes.
- The text references "Fig. III-12" for alternative panel forms.

pages.summary:
This page provides an introduction to slipform technology, a method for vertically extruding reinforced concrete sections used in high-rise structures like lift shafts, stair shafts, and towers. The text describes the process where formwork rises continuously at a rate of about 300 mm per hour, supporting itself on the core without external support. It highlights that concrete is poured continuously into walls until the required height is reached, with the lowest layer gaining initial set before the formwork moves upward. A photograph on the right shows the Cheung Kong Centre under construction using this technique.

**Text Evidence:**
- Slipform technology is a method for vertically extruding reinforced concrete sections.
- Suitable for construction of core walls in high-rise structures including lift shafts, stair shafts, and towers.
- Formwork rises continuously at a rate of about 300 mm per hour.
- The formwork supports itself on the core and does not rely on support from other parts of the building.
- Allows continuous pouring of concrete into walls until the full required height is reached.
- The formwork design ensures the lowest layer of concrete has gained an initial set before the formwork moves up.

**Visual Evidence:**
<image_summary>Cheung Kong Centre: Aerial photograph showing a high-rise building under construction with visible slipform technology in use. pages.ocr_text: ADVANTAGES:
pages.summary:
This page outlines the advantages of slipform building construction compared to traditional concrete structure methods. It highlights that a major cost in conventional construction is the required formwork, which must be continuously removed and re-erected, leading to high labor and equipment costs. In contrast, slipform construction erects the formwork only once, resulting in significant cost and time savings, reduced labor expenses for intermittent concreting, and improved safety by minimizing the movement of formwork and workers. A diagram on the right illustrates the slipform system with its structural components.

**Text Evidence:**
- A major cost of concrete structure construction is the required formwork to retain concrete until it can be safely de-shuttered.
- Formwork needs to be continually removed and re-erected in traditional methods.
- Continuous use of manpower and lifting equipment like cranes is required.
- In slipform building, formwork is erected only once and remains intact until completion.
- Slipform offers great reduction in formwork cost and time saving for re-erection.
- It is cost-effective and saves on labor costs for intermittent concreting operations.
- The reduction in formwork movement leads to far more safe working conditions.

**Visual Evidence:**
<figure_summary>Figure 1: Diagram of a slipform building system - shows a large, continuous formwork structure (orange) surrounding two vertical concrete columns (gray). The formwork is supported by a framework and includes platforms and guide rails, illustrating how it moves upward as concrete is poured.</figure_summary>

pages.ocr_text: TUNNEL FORMWORK SYSTEM
pages.summary:
This page introduces the Tunnel Formwork System, a modern construction method (MMC) that enables contractors to cast walls and slabs in a single daily operation. It highlights the system's ability to combine the speed, quality, and accuracy of factory production with the flexibility and economy of on-site construction. The page features a large photograph showing the system in use at a construction site, where red formwork panels are installed around rebar cages for concrete pouring. The text emphasizes its recognition as a leading technique in contemporary building practices.

**Text Evidence:**
- Tunnel formwork system allows casting of walls and slabs in one operation per day.
- Combines the speed, quality, and accuracy of factory/off-site production with the flexibility and economy of in-situ construction.
- Recognized as a modern method of construction (MMC).

**Visual Evidence:**
<image_summary>Photo of a construction site showing a tunnel formwork system in place. Red modular formwork panels are assembled around rebar cages for concrete pouring. Workers are visible on the site, and the structure appears to be a multi-level foundation or basement slab. The image illustrates the system's application in creating large, continuous concrete elements.</image_summary>

pages.summary:
This page discusses safety features of metal formwork systems, highlighting that they can include integral concreting platforms with guard rails and ladders, reducing the need for independent access. It contrasts this with disposable formwork systems, which require separate working platforms and pose safety risks when columns are at building edges or corners. The text notes that some formwork systems require work from only one side, which could be a safety consideration, and emphasizes that metal systems typically provide robust assemblies with simple assembly processes that minimize power tool use. A 3D illustration on the right shows a metal formwork system in use with workers on platforms.

**Text Evidence:**
- Metal formwork systems can have integral ready-to-use concreting platforms with guard rails and access equipment including ladders.
- This reduces the need for independent access.
- For systems with disposable formwork, working platforms must be erected separately to allow safe access to the top of column forms.
- Formwork systems are available which need to be worked only from one side, which could be an important safety consideration for columns at building edges and corners.
- Metal systems typically provide robust assemblies.
- Assembly process is simple, allowing site operatives to become familiar with health and safety aspects.
- These formwork systems normally require minimal use of power tools.

**Visual Evidence:**

The entire setup is shown on a grey concrete base.</image_summary>

This page, titled "DRAWBACKS," outlines the disadvantages of pre-fabricated formwork in construction. It lists several key issues including high cost due to transportation challenges and the complexity of handling numerous pieces. The text highlights that pre-fabricated formwork often results in poor finishes at joints and can deflect during placement, with the rate of placing being a primary cause. However, it also notes that these problems can be mitigated with proper supervision and techniques like vibrating. A photograph on the right side shows a stack of pre-fabricated formwork panels, illustrating the physical product being discussed.

- High cost factor due to greater transportation costs for large pieces
- Pre-fabricated formwork involves too many pieces and leaves poor finishes at joints
- Deflection during placement is a major issue, primarily caused by a fast rate of placing
- Proper supervision and vibrating can control deflection problems
- Panels can be re-moved and reused as casting pockets

pages.ocr_text: DRAWBACKS
pages.summary:
This page, titled "DRAWBACKS," outlines the disadvantages of pre-fabricated formwork in construction. It lists several key issues including high cost due to transportation challenges and the complexity of handling numerous pieces. The text highlights that pre-fabricated formwork often results in poor finishes at joints and can deflect during placement, with the rate of placing being a primary cause. However, it also notes that these problems can be mitigated with proper supervision and techniques like vibrating. A photograph on the right side shows a stack of pre-fabricated formwork panels, illustrating the physical product being discussed.

**Text Evidence:**
- High cost factor due to greater transportation costs for large pieces
- Pre-fabricated formwork involves too many pieces and leaves poor finishes at joints
- Deflection during placement is a major issue, primarily caused by a fast rate of placing
- Proper supervision and vibrating can control deflection problems
- Panels can be re-moved and reused as casting pockets

This page discusses the causes of formwork failures during concrete construction, emphasizing that such failures often result from a chain reaction initiated by an unexpected event. The text lists several contributing factors including improper stripping, inadequate bracing, vibration, unstable soil, and poor control of concrete placement. Two photographs on the right side illustrate real-world examples of collapsed formwork structures, showing extensive damage to the scaffolding and concrete slabs. The page highlights that vibrations from passing traffic, worker movement, equipment, and concrete consolidation can displace shores or jacks, leading to collapse.

**Text Evidence:**
- Formwork failures are a major cause of accidents during concrete construction
- Failures typically occur when fresh concrete is placed
- A single member failure can lead to overload or misalignment causing total collapse
- Key causes include improper stripping, inadequate bracing, vibration, unstable soil, and lack of attention to details
- Forms can collapse when shores/jacks are displaced by vibrations from traffic, workers/equipment, or vibrating concrete

**Visual Evidence:**
<image_summary>Top photograph: Shows a large-scale formwork collapse on a construction site with damaged concrete slab and exposed rebar. The structure appears to have partially collapsed, with debris scattered around. The surrounding area includes other construction elements like scaffolding and building walls.</image_summary>
<image_summary>Bottom photograph: Depicts another formwork failure with a network of collapsed metal supports and wooden planks. The image shows a complex web of failed shoring systems, indicating structural instability. The scene includes vertical columns and horizontal beams in disarray.</image_summary>

elements.text: Formwork failures are the cause of many accidents and failures that occur during concrete construction which usually happen when fresh concrete is placed
Generally some unexpected event causes one member to fail, then others become overloaded or misaligned and the entire formwork structure collapses
Unstable soil under mugsills, shoring not plumb
Lack of attention to formwork details
Inadequate cross bracing and horizontal bracing of shores
Forms sometime collapse when their shores/ jack are displaced by the vibration caused by:
movement of workers & equipment on the formwork
the effect of vibrating concrete to consolidate it

- Column and beam side formwork must be removed before beam and slab soffit formwork. (Page 59)
- Permanent propping or shoring is required if beam and slab soffit formwork is removed before concrete achieves working strength. (Page 59)

This page provides guidelines for the striking, maintenance, and storage of formwork in construction. It details the correct sequence for removing formwork, emphasizing that column and beam side formwork should be removed before beam and slab soffit formwork to ensure structural safety. The text specifies that permanent propping or shoring is required if soffit formwork is removed prematurely. Maintenance instructions include cleaning with a stiff brush and cold water, using scrapers only as a last resort, and oiling edges to prevent damage. For storage, formwork with steel components must be kept dry, protected from direct sunlight, and stored clear of the ground without twist or bend. The document notes that timber formwork can achieve eight or more uses.
